projects.title: Kiwi Swerve Drivetrain
projects.summary: Dorito reuses the pods from my FTC coaxial swerve project after selling them stopped making sense.
projects.cardSummary: Dorito is a three module Kiwi swerve drivetrain I designed and built from general purpose parts, with continuous rotation steering servos, absolute encoders, and Python code on a Raspberry Pi. Three modules instead of four cut the cost and parts count of a normal swerve drive while keeping full movement in any direction. On the first robot the belts slipped and the drive shaft bearings broke under high load. It drives sideways, spins, and moves diagonally, and those two problems aren't fixed yet, which is what V2 is for.
projects.imageAlt: A three-module Kiwi swerve drivetrain prototype with a white 3D-printed frame and battery, sitting inside a taped test field.
projects.motionImageAlt: Animation of the Kiwi swerve drivetrain driving and turning across a floor.

overview.problem: A normal swerve drive needs four modules and all the motors, drivers, and gearing that come with them. I wanted a cheaper complete swerve drivetrain for robotics, assistive platforms, and teaching, built from pods I already had.
overview.method: I designed a triangular chassis with three matching modules 120 degrees apart, which removes a quarter of the actuators, drivers, and gearing. The gears and bearings are COTS parts available from more than one seller, and I programmed the robot in Python on a Raspberry Pi 4.
overview.result: The first prototype drives sideways, spins, and moves diagonally, which proves the three module layout. It isn't finished, since the drive hardware still needs work, and V2 is in progress now.

sections.heading: Where Dorito Came From
sections.body: I had been developing my coaxial pod into a product for FTC teams, but FTC announced a move away from the brushed DC motors and standalone servos it was built around. Instead of building a product around outgoing hardware, I built Dorito as a complete chassis from general purpose parts.

sections.heading: First Prototype Build
sections.body: I 3D printed the smaller parts and CNC cut the aluminum plates, with M4 hardware on most of the chassis and M3 on the smaller pieces. Each pod steers with a continuous rotation servo through an HTD5 belt, a lighter HTD2 belt drives the wheel, and a 12 bit encoder reads the pod's angle. Both motors stay fixed in the chassis, so the pods turn a full 360 degrees with no hard stop.

sections.heading: Electronics and Code
sections.body: The robot runs on a Raspberry Pi 4 with three 10 amp motor drivers, a servo HAT, and a 12 bit encoder board, chosen for what the robot needed and how easy they are to replace. The code turns driver or autonomous commands into a speed and angle for each module, corrects each servo against its encoder, and limits combined motor current so the battery doesn't brown out.

sections.heading: Slipping Belts and Broken Bearings
sections.body: Driving tests showed two weak spots. The belts slipped, and the drive shaft bearings broke under high load. Steering response, encoder feedback, and the triangular layout all held up, so the problems are in the drive hardware, not the concept. These two aren't fixed yet. The second robot I'm working on now keeps the mechanical design, electronics, and code from the first prototype and is built around fixing the belt slip and the bearings.

projects.title: AI Eye Animatronic Chatbot
projects.summary: After high school robotics I wanted to get into animatronics, and an eye was a good first project.
projects.cardSummary: This is a four servo animatronic eye on a monitor arm that I built into a voice assistant, so it listens, answers out loud, blinks, and looks around while it talks. The assistant gave the eye's movement a purpose instead of a looping display. In testing the upper eyelid pivot broke, and stiff servo moves made noise right next to the microphone. I reinforced the lid pivots and added cosine easing to every servo move, and it now holds a full conversation and can be interrupted mid answer.
projects.imageAlt: A large 3D-printed animatronic eyeball in green and black, mounted on a desk.

overview.problem: A moving eye combines mechanical design, motion control, and software in a small system. Once it worked mechanically it only repeated motion, so I wanted it to react to someone talking to it.
overview.method: I based the mechanism on a GrabCAD eye animatronic and built it between April 10 and 18, 2025. A Raspberry Pi drives the four servos through a PCA9685 board and runs the whole conversation.
overview.result: It met the goal. It holds a conversation while blinking and moving the eye, and interrupting it doesn't leave the mechanism in a strange position. The project is finished, and the code and STEP file are public.

sections.heading: Building the Eye
sections.body: Two servos inside the eyeball tilt it up and down and pan it left and right. Two more drive the upper and lower eyelids through short linkages. A central bolt mounts it all to a spare monitor arm, with the upper lid servo on four holes already in the arm.

sections.heading: Adding the Assistant
sections.body: After the wake phrase, the Pi transcribes speech with Google speech recognition, sends it to OpenAI's gpt-3.5-turbo, and speaks the reply with Google text to speech. When idle the lids stay closed and the eye centered, and on waking it opens, double blinks, and looks around at random. It keeps listening while it talks, so the wake phrase or goodbye cuts the answer off and it returns to listening.

sections.heading: Broken Pivots and Colliding Lids
sections.body: The parts sticking out of the arm mount were too fragile in early versions, so I thickened them. Then the upper eyelid pivot broke in testing, so I reinforced the upper lid linkage and made the lower lid pivot about 5 mm thicker, with a longer linkage for the more distant servo. Both lids rotate around the same area and could collide, so I added a relief slot that lets the upper lid nest into the lower lid's area.

sections.heading: Stiff, Noisy Motion
sections.body: Linear servo moves looked mechanical, and their hard starts and stops made noise right next to the microphone, which can interfere with speech recognition. I made every servo move ease in and out on a cosine curve, which looks natural and runs quieter. Each servo also has calibrated limits backed off from its hard stops and runs on its own supply with a common ground to the Pi.

projects.title: Coaxial Swerve Drive
projects.summary: I wanted to sell a compact swerve pod that FTC teams could put on a robot without designing their own.
projects.cardSummary: I designed a coaxial swerve pod for FTC that fits a full drive and steering module inside a four inch cube, with one motor for the wheel and one servo for steering. The goal was swerve that FTC teams could afford and bolt onto their robots. V1 worked, but custom shafts, a printed housing, and specialized parts pushed one module to nearly $400, so V2 switched to standard gears, bearings, and shafts with GoBILDA, REV, and AndyMark mounting patterns. I ended the product plan when FTC announced a move away from the brushed motors and standalone servos the pod was built around.
projects.imageAlt: A coaxial swerve drive module bolted to an aluminium test chassis with motors and wiring, photographed on a desk.
projects.motionImageAlt: Animation of a coaxial swerve robot driving and spinning on a competition field.

overview.problem: Swerve steers normal rubber wheels instead of rollers, so it keeps full pushing force, but it is usually expensive and hard to fit in an 18 inch FTC chassis. The pod had to be small enough to package and cheap enough for teams to realistically use four.
overview.method: V1 proved the coaxial layout could work at this size. V2 kept the concept and replaced as many custom parts as possible with ones teams could easily source and replace.
overview.result: V2 was easier to manufacture and integrate and far more practical than V1, but it never became a product. The project is finished, and the CAD and notes are public as a reference for compact swerve packaging.

sections.heading: V1 in a Four Inch Cube
sections.body: V1 packs coaxial bevel gears, thrust bearings, and two shafts into an L shaped housing. Drive power passes through the center of the rotating module, so the wheel steers without interfering with the drive. Bench testing proved the compact layout worked.

sections.heading: The $400 Problem
sections.body: V1 worked, but the custom turned shafts, complicated printed housing, and specialized hardware brought one module to nearly $400. At that price a four module drivetrain was unrealistic for most FTC teams. For V2 I redesigned the L shaped housing into a simpler rectangular module built around off the shelf gears, bearings, and shafts, under about 4.25 inches tall. GoBILDA 16mm, REV 8mm, and AndyMark mounting patterns let teams on any of those systems mount it without custom adapters, and drive and module tests of the second prototype are on YouTube.

sections.heading: Why I Stopped the Product
sections.body: During V2, FTC announced a transition from brushed DC motors and standalone servos to a new actuator system. Redesigning around hardware that wasn't established yet didn't make sense, so I stopped the commercial version and carried the pods into Dorito, my three module Kiwi swerve chassis.

projects.title: Simple Swerve Drive
projects.summary: I started this right after the 2023 to 2024 NYC FTC Championship to get hands on experience with swerve.
projects.cardSummary: Simple Swerve is a differential swerve drivetrain I designed for FTC, where the same two motors in each pod both drive and steer the wheel. It was a way to try swerve without the cost and packaging of a full four module setup. My first chassis measured 18.25 inches wide, over the 18 inch limit. Turning the motors 90 degrees with right angle gearboxes brought it inside the limit as a compact two pod drivetrain.
projects.imageAlt: A differential swerve drivetrain on a workbench, with four modules, green wheels and paired motors.

overview.problem: A traditional four module swerve is expensive and hard to package inside FTC's 18 inch limit. Differential swerve cuts down the hardware because each pod's two motors share driving and steering.
overview.method: I started from FTC 11115's differential design and simplified the gearbox. I built and filmed a first prototype on March 4, 2024, then reworked the layout until it fit FTC sizing, saving each version as its own CAD release.
overview.result: It met the goal. The FTC sized version was running on video by March 20, 2024, and the project closed after four CAD versions.

sections.heading: How Differential Swerve Works
sections.body: When a pod's two motors spin the same way the wheel drives, and when they spin at different speeds the pod turns. That keeps full wheel traction, which mecanum and omni drives give up to move sideways.

sections.heading: Simplifying the Gearbox
sections.body: Differential gearboxes usually need a lot of machining, and set screws on D shafts tend to slip. I rebuilt the gear stack around M3x45 bolts with ball bearings inside the printed gears, so there are no D bores at all.

sections.heading: 18.25 Inches Wide
sections.body: My first complete layout came out at 18.25 inches, a quarter inch over the limit, so it would not pass inspection. The prototype had already proven the differential worked, so I rotated the motors 90 degrees with REV Ultra 90 gearboxes, which brought the width inside the limit, and cut the powered pods to two with passive omni wheels at the four corners. That became V1.

sections.heading: V2 and the Four Releases
sections.body: V2 went back to more efficient inline motors with no bevel stage, with versions for REV UltraPlanetary and GoBILDA Yellow Jacket motors. The repository keeps all four CAD releases and the development pictures.

projects.title: FTC 9384 Robot: EggWUUUHH
projects.summary: This was Team 9384's CENTERSTAGE robot and my last FTC robot in high school.
projects.cardSummary: EggWUUUHH was FTC Team 9384's CENTERSTAGE robot, built to collect pixels, score them on the backdrop, launch the paper plane, and climb, all on one 18 inch robot. Nearly every mechanism had a problem at first, from intake servos too weak to run the wheels to an outtake that couldn't release pixels at the backdrop's angle. We rebuilt it four times in one season, fixing each problem in the mechanism itself. The final version handled every major task and ranked 12th at the NYC Championship.
projects.imageAlt: FTC competition robot EggWUUUHH seen from the front, showing linear slides, green wiring and a yellow intake.

overview.problem: Each CENTERSTAGE task needed its own mechanism, including scoring on an angled backdrop and launching the plane during endgame. The hard part was fitting all of them on one 18x18x18 robot without them interfering.
overview.method: We treated the robot as a design that would change all season. When testing showed a jam, a weak part, or a misalignment, we fixed the mechanical design instead of covering for it in software, and spent our time on whatever limited scoring.
overview.result: Version four was the most complete and reliable robot of our season and ranked 12th at the NYC Championship. The CAD, engineering portfolio, and notebook are public and show the full progression.

sections.heading: Chassis and Lift
sections.body: The robot ran a mecanum drivetrain on a custom chassis of four parallel aluminum plates tied together with extrusions. The lift was stacked drawer slides pulled by one motor and a string, with 3D printed spacers that double as pulley supports. Magnetic limit switches at each end told the code where the lift stopped.

sections.heading: Intake, Launcher and Climber
sections.body: The intake moved pixels in three stages, with star wheels to grab, counter rotating rollers to pull, and zip ties to sweep them into the outtake. A spring powered launcher fired the plane, with one servo to release it and one to set the angle. The climber was a winch pulling pivoting hooks, reset by rubber bands.

sections.heading: The Intake Redesign Before Our First Competition
sections.body: The first intake lifted a linkage with two servos, and the wheels were too heavy for them, which also hurt the transfer into the outtake. We redesigned it the day before our first competition into the roller and star wheel version we kept.

sections.heading: An Outtake That Couldn't Score
sections.body: The outtake took the most rework. A sloped design didn't move pixels, and a box with printed belts was fast but couldn't release at the backdrop's angle, so it failed at our first competition. We adapted the pivoting box from our 2021 Freight Frenzy robot so each pixel slides onto the backdrop, then added a servo finger to hold one pixel while the other scores.

sections.heading: Slides, Brackets and Hooks
sections.body: The REV slides' plastic guides caused friction and made the slide snap, so we switched to ball bearing drawer slides and added 95A TPU braces when they sagged under load. Small plastic L brackets let the chassis flex until three full span extrusions with metal brackets fixed it. We lengthened the climber hook tip so it caught the truss every time.

sections.heading: Four Versions
sections.body: Version two was mostly the new outtake, version three added a servo hook on the intake to pull pixels off the stack in autonomous, and version four added the climber. The stack hook took three tries and ended up with toy car wheels on a brass rod for grip.

projects.title: Tubba Odometry Pods
projects.summary: Few small FTC odometry pods were available to buy at the time, so I designed our own.
projects.cardSummary: Tubba is a dead wheel odometry pod I designed for EggWUUUHH, FTC Team 9384's 2023 to 2024 CENTERSTAGE robot. A spring holds a two inch omni wheel on the field while a through bore encoder reads it, so drivetrain slip doesn't throw off the position estimate. The first pods pivoted on a swing arm that caught on pixels, and the pivot screw kept bending. I moved the spring inside the pod so the wheel moves straight up and down, replaced the screw with a hex shaft, and we ran three in competition.
projects.imageAlt: CAD render of the Tubba dead-wheel odometry pod assembly.

overview.problem: The small pods available were expensive, awkward to fit, or still needed custom parts. We needed odometry so autonomous could track the robot's real position instead of estimating from powered wheels that slip.
overview.method: I designed the pod around a two inch AndyMark Dualie omni wheel and a REV Through Bore encoder, with printed plates, a hex shaft, a bearing, and surgical tubing for preload. It started as an offseason project and kept changing once it was on the chassis. I also helped calibrate the conversion from encoder ticks to inches.
overview.result: Three pods ran on the robot through competition, at about $100 each in 2024. They gave the code a steadier position estimate and made our autonomous paths more repeatable. The CAD and parts list are public.

sections.heading: Building the First Pod
sections.body: The first case started from a GrabCAD design that was easy to extend, so I could fit a larger omni wheel than the standard REV one for better traction. I added an end bearing for smoother rotation and capped the bearings against dust. The encoder reads the free spinning wheel at 8192 counts per revolution, and the PLA test print held up well enough that we kept PLA for the final robot.

sections.heading: Bent Screws and Bolts in the Way
sections.body: On the chassis, protruding nuts and bolts got in the way of mounting, so I added pockets for them. The pivot screw often bent and threw off the readings, and a 5mm hex shaft fixed that.

sections.heading: Catching on Pixels
sections.body: The swing arm layout on the sides and back of the chassis caught on pixels when the robot drove over them, which wasn't going to work for the game. For the final pod I kept the same wheel and encoder but moved the suspension inside the pod, so the spring moves the wheel straight up and down. That stopped it catching on pixels and made it compact enough to fit between the robot's parallel plates. Two pods sit inside the chassis and one at the back, and the code turns their ticks into an x and y position for autonomous paths.

projects.title: FTC 9384 Robot: Crabby
projects.summary: We needed a robot that could cycle cones onto POWERPLAY's junctions quickly and accurately.
projects.cardSummary: Crabby was FTC Team 9384's POWERPLAY robot and my first full FTC robot where I led much of the mechanical development. It had to place cones on junctions of different heights quickly, without swaying or turning the whole robot to aim. The first version's single slide swayed at full height and its wheel intake couldn't keep cones upright. Over three rebuilds we added a claw, a direct drive turret, and a second slide, and the final version placed 9th at the state championship.
projects.imageAlt: FTC competition robot Crabby, with a vertical lift and cone intake, photographed outdoors at night.

overview.problem: Fast cycling meant the drivetrain, lift, turret, and intake had to work together. Speed didn't matter if the chassis moved during scoring or lift flex made the cone miss the junction.
overview.method: We rebuilt the robot three times between kickoff on September 10, 2022 and the state championship, each time targeting what failed, flexed, or was too slow in testing or competition.
overview.result: The final version was lower, more rigid, and much more consistent than the first, and it placed 9th at the state championship.

sections.heading: The First Robot
sections.body: Version one put a single REV linear slide on an H shaped mecanum chassis of aluminum C channels and L brackets, based on REV's mecanum kit. The intake hung from the slide's last stage and gripped cones between two compliant wheels on servos.

sections.heading: Cones Falling Out
sections.body: The wheel intake could pull in a centered cone smoothly, but it didn't reliably keep cones upright or stop them falling out. In version two we replaced it with a claw, which solved the cone problem for the rest of the season, so version three kept it.

sections.heading: Turning the Whole Robot to Aim
sections.body: The lift was slow, and because it was fixed to the chassis the robot had to turn to face every junction before scoring. Version two regeared the slide motor for speed and mounted the lift on a lazy Susan turret driven directly by a motor shaft at its center, so the lift could aim without turning the chassis. We weren't aware of any earlier FTC robot driving a turret that way.

sections.heading: Sway at Full Height
sections.body: The tall single slide swayed at full extension when the chassis moved, which could drop the cone. Version three added a second slide to square the lift and cut the sway, on a larger lazy Susan that could carry both slides. Four 90 degree bevel gearboxes also moved the drive motors inside the C channels so the chassis sat lower, and extra cross members kept the turret base square.

projects.title: OmniBot
projects.summary: OmniBot is the club robot I wish we had when I was first learning coding.
projects.cardSummary: OmniBot is a three omni wheel teaching robot we built for the City Tech AI & Automation Club, with parts under $100 and a mostly printed structure. I programmed its drive code, its Wi-Fi dashboard and a one command installer, and it drives from that dashboard or a Bluetooth controller. The hardest part was getting the installer to run cleanly on a fresh Raspberry Pi, which took several rounds of fixes for package and certificate errors. Now one command sets up the whole robot, and local image recognition is still being developed.
projects.imageAlt: The assembled OmniBot, a black triangular robot with three omni wheels, on a wooden floor.

overview.problem: A closed commercial kit doesn't let students see or change how the robot works. We wanted a cheap robot students could build, take apart, reprogram and improve, covering omni drive code, motors, servos, CAD, 3D printing, Raspberry Pi programming and basic vision on one platform.
overview.method: We designed a printed three wheel chassis with custom omni wheels and put a Raspberry Pi 4 in charge of three motor drivers, a PCA9685 servo HAT, and a USB webcam. I wrote the drive code, the Wi-Fi dashboard, and an installer that sets up the whole robot from a single command.
overview.result: OmniBot drives, strafes and rotates from either the controller or the dashboard, and the CAD, code, tests and installer are all open in the repo. The vision part is still being developed and isn't in the installer yet.

sections.heading: Printing the Chassis and Wheels
sections.body: Almost every structural part is printed, including the chassis, mounts, wheel bodies and rollers. The chassis prints in three sections joined underneath, so it fits a normal desktop printer and one section can be replaced on its own. The rigid wheel bodies carry TPU rollers that grip enough to drive but slip a little on rubber field tiles, which keeps rubber on rubber friction from loading the small motors. Heat set inserts let it be assembled and taken apart over and over.

sections.heading: Drive Code and Controls
sections.body: The three wheels sit 120 degrees apart, and the drive math mixes forward, strafe and rotation into a power for each motor. The code gives the motors a short 100% breakaway pulse before shaped 75 to 100% output, and coasts for 80 ms before reversing one. The dashboard only arms after Enable is pressed with the controls held neutral for 0.25 seconds, and the Pi stops the motors if commands stop for 200 ms.

sections.heading: Getting the Installer to Work
sections.body: The installer took many rounds to get right. It kept failing on a fresh Pi during package setup, so I changed it to install and report each package separately and print the last 30 apt lines with the OS and clock details when one fails. Certificate errors also showed up when the Pi's clock was wrong, so it now syncs the clock and rebuilds the certificates itself instead of turning off verification.

sections.heading: Camera and Screen Fixes
sections.body: The robot also had to work with whatever generic USB webcam is plugged in, and different cameras show up at different device paths. The camera code tries the stable paths first, falls back through every usable video device, and reconnects on its own if the webcam is unplugged, while driving keeps working. The Pygame interface on the 800x480 onboard screen also covered the Raspberry Pi desktop panel, so it now leaves the top 40 pixels free.

sections.heading: Where It Stands
sections.body: Rerunning the same command also handles updates. It only installs what is missing, rolls back to the previous version if a new one fails its tests, and never reboots after a failed check. The chassis can still flex a little when lifted because of how the three sections join underneath, and that isn't fixed yet. The next step for the software is lightweight image recognition that runs locally on the Pi instead of through a large language model.

projects.title: Digital Camera
projects.summary: I wanted a camera I built myself that didn't need a phone or computer to see what I took.
projects.cardSummary: aloeZ mini mini is a small ESP32-S3 camera I designed with a live viewfinder, a photo gallery, and a printed case. My first version took photos but had no screen, so V2 moved to a Freenove Media Kit to frame and review shots on the camera itself. The hard part was the battery, since the connector polarity was reversed and the reading jumped from 96% on USB to about 40% the moment I unplugged. I logged and analyzed the readings and changed the display to a filtered live estimate marked with a ~, which is still only an estimate.
projects.imageAlt: The assembled aloeZ mini mini camera in its printed case.

overview.problem: V1 had no screen, so I couldn't see what I was pointing at, and photos could only be viewed over Wi-Fi. V2 had to frame and review shots on the camera itself, running on its own battery.
overview.method: I moved from a XIAO ESP32S3 Sense to a Freenove ESP32-S3 Media Kit with a 1.14 inch display and five way control. I programmed the camera interface and designed an enclosure in Fusion 360 for the board and a 1500 mAh LiPo.
overview.result: V2 meets the main goal with a live viewfinder and playback on its own battery. The battery percentage is still a voltage estimate, not a true measure of remaining charge.

sections.heading: First Camera
sections.body: V1 ran on a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32S3 Sense with a power switch, shutter button, and LED I added, and it served photos on a Wi-Fi download page.

sections.heading: Adding a Screen
sections.body: The Media Kit already had a camera, display, MicroSD slot, and physical controls on one board. The center control takes a photo, and photos save to MicroSD as BMP files. Playback opens the newest photo first and can switch to an eight photo grid.

sections.heading: Case and Battery
sections.body: The case fits the board, screen, controls, and a KBT 883545PL 3.7 V 1500 mAh LiPo, and the STEP and Fusion 360 files are public. The battery's connector polarity was reversed for the Media Kit and had to be corrected, so the docs now warn to check positive to positive.

sections.heading: The Battery Reading
sections.body: Battery percentage was the hardest problem. In 73 logged samples the reading was about 4.17 V and 96% on USB, then dropped right away to about 3.76 V and 40 to 42% on battery, a jump of around 408 mV caused by the power condition, not lost charge. The schematic showed the ADC reads a node behind a transistor, and no pin tells the firmware about USB power or charging. So instead of a fixed percentage the display shows a filtered live estimate marked with ~, sampled in the background and trimmed of spikes, and it shows --% while readings are noisy or settling.

sections.heading: Still an Estimate
sections.body: It doesn't fake a percentage while charging, since the board's blue LED shows that instead. Serial commands record battery tests to the card, with steps for calibrating against a multimeter, but the number is still only an estimate.
