projects.title: TrainUI XL
projects.summary: I wanted a screen in my room that tells me when the next train is coming at a glance.
projects.cardSummary: TrainUI XL is a full size NYC subway departure board I built for my desk, running on a Raspberry Pi Zero W with a 10.1 inch screen and a 3D printed frame. It shows live MTA arrivals, alerts, weather, and Pi health, so I can check the next train without opening an app. The hardest part was making it run all day unattended, since text was cut off on the panel and the display could freeze. I rebuilt the layout so every label wraps to its real space, and added a heartbeat watchdog that restarts the app if the clock stops updating.
projects.imageAlt: The TrainUI XL departure board showing live New York City subway arrivals, a service alert, weather and system health readouts.

overview.problem: Checking trains meant opening a phone app. I also wanted it to look like finished furniture rather than a Raspberry Pi with wires hanging off it, and to start on its own every time it powers on.
overview.method: I wrote a fullscreen Python interface for the original Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the MTA's public realtime feeds, with no account or API key. I designed a three layer printed case around the screen and Pi, and wrote a one command installer that sets the train and station and starts everything on boot.
overview.result: It runs through the day without being touched. The installer, assembly guide, BOM, and CAD are public so others can build one, and I also made a Trackside layout for a bar with a bigger clock and a five day forecast.

sections.heading: The Frame and Shell
sections.body: The case splits into a faceplate, middle plate, and back plate so it prints on common desktop printers while staying rigid enough for the 10.1 inch display. Heat set inserts and four M3 by 25 mm screws close it, the Pi mounts only one way, and a keyhole slot hangs it on a drywall screw. An optional outer shell hides the joints and layer lines and can be swapped for wood or decorative panels.

sections.heading: What the Board Shows
sections.body: The main screen shows arrivals in both directions for the chosen station from the MTA's GTFS realtime feeds, along with service status and alerts for that route. Beside them are New York City weather, the time, Wi-Fi status, and the Pi's system health. An optional daily sleep schedule powers down only the display, so it wakes straight back into the board.

sections.heading: Text Getting Cut Off
sections.body: On the real 600 by 1024 panel, text was clipped in four ways. A three character limit cut the E off DUE, a truncate helper chopped the weather line and Wi-Fi name, font sizing was measured against the full screen width instead of each label's column, and fixed card heights cropped anything that grew. I replaced all four with one wrapping label that sizes text to the space it actually gets, and a test renders both boards at panel size and fails if anything clips.

sections.heading: Freezes
sections.body: The board is meant to run for days, but a stuck clock or crash meant walking over to restart it. Now the app writes a heartbeat on every clock update and the launcher restarts it if that goes stale for 45 seconds, with a daily restart and the Pi's hardware watchdog as backups.

sections.heading: Lost Wi-Fi
sections.body: Losing Wi-Fi had the same problem, since there is no keyboard on the Pi to fix the connection. If the Pi is offline for 30 seconds it now starts a TrainUI hotspot with a setup page, and the screen shows how to join it only while the hotspot is on.

projects.title: ZeroG Hydra 3D Printer
projects.summary: After modifying several smaller printers, I wanted to build a larger machine of my own, and when I started around the time the X1C came out, this setup was very advanced.
projects.cardSummary: Hydra is a large custom CoreXY 3D printer I am building around the ZeroG Mercury One.1 motion system and the Hydra three point bed. The goal is a big machine that keeps good print quality without manual setup before every print. Instead of leveling knobs, Klipper drives each of the three Z points independently and a Beacon eddy current probe scans the bed for the first layer. The motion, bed, probing, and electronics are working, and the machine is still being finished and tuned.
projects.imageAlt: The ZeroG Hydra CoreXY 3D printer part-built, showing its aluminium extrusion frame and illuminated toolhead.

overview.problem: I wanted a printer focused on print quality over a large build area, automatic calibration, easier maintenance, and useful sensors, not only speed. The goal was to cut the setup needed before each print.
overview.method: I designed it around a rigid CoreXY motion system and a bed on three independently driven points, with Beacon probing, a filament cutting toolhead, and an electronics bay running Klipper underneath. I wrote the Klipper config, macros, Beacon setup, RGB control, adaptive bed mesh, and an OrcaSlicer profile.
overview.result: It is partly there. The CoreXY motion, automatic three point bed adjustment, probing, electronics, and monitoring hardware work, and the hotend and bed have tuned PID values. What remains is finishing the machine and tuning the systems together.

sections.heading: Motion and Bed
sections.body: Both XY motors stay fixed on the rear of the frame and the belts move the toolhead, which keeps moving mass low. On startup Klipper probes the bed's three pivots with the Beacon and moves each Z stepper separately to square the bed to the gantry, then builds an adaptive mesh over just the print area. The Beacon measures by eddy current without touching the bed and doubles as the input shaping accelerometer.

sections.heading: Electronics Bay
sections.body: A ventilated bay under the bed holds the main controller, a USB hub for the Beacon and toolhead boards, a 24 V power supply, the Linux computer running Klipper, and a solid state relay for the 110 V heated bed. Running the bed heater off mains through the relay lets it heat quickly, and keeping everything in one bay makes the printer easier to service.

sections.heading: The Toolhead
sections.body: The toolhead is based on the Filametrix filament cutting system, with a Phaetus Rapido high flow hotend and a Clockwork 2 direct drive extruder. One filament sensor above the extruder pauses on runout, and a second below the cutter confirms the filament was cut and pulled back. It also carries the Beacon probe, RGB lighting, and a small status display.

projects.title: Self Balancing Robot
projects.summary: PID control is easy to write down and hard to actually feel, and we wanted a project that changed that.
projects.cardSummary: We built three self balancing robots from parts available at school so the club could see PID control working instead of only reading the equation. Each reads its tilt from an MPU6050 and drives two DC motors to keep the wheels under its center of mass. The hard part was getting the motors to correct by the right amount, and none of the robots balanced best at exactly zero degrees. PID tuning, a tuned target angle, minimum motor power and moving weight around the chassis got all three versions balancing.
projects.imageAlt: A two-wheeled self-balancing robot on a laser-cut chassis with an Arduino, breadboard and coloured jumper wires.

overview.problem: A balancing robot either stays upright or it falls, so every gain value and every part you move shows its effect immediately. It could also be built from hardware the school already had.
overview.method: We built three versions: a reused prototype chassis, a custom 3D printed body, and a Raspberry Pi Pico version. Each uses an MPU6050, a dual H-bridge, and two geared DC motors, with firmware for the Arduino Nano and the Pico plus earlier motor, IMU, and PID experiments.
overview.result: All three prototypes balance and drive forward and backward under control. The repo keeps the working firmware and the earlier experiments so club members can see how the control code changed and change it themselves.

sections.heading: Three Versions
sections.body: Version 1 used a modified car chassis to check the sensor orientation, the motor directions and the first balance corrections. Version 2 moved to a custom printed body to place the components better and put the center of gravity where we wanted it. Version 3 switched to a Raspberry Pi Pico to test faster loop timing and smoother motor response. Every version kept the MPU6050 and H-bridge, so the control problem stayed the same while the hardware changed.

sections.heading: Reading the Angle
sections.body: A complementary filter combines the MPU6050's accelerometer and gyroscope data over I2C, trusting the gyro for fast changes and the accelerometer for the long term angle, with the final firmware weighting the gyro at 0.99 or 0.995. On the Nano the sensor ended up mounted the other way, so the code flips the math. This mattered more than anything else, because even a small angle error makes the robot think it is leaning when it is upright.

sections.heading: The Tuning Problem
sections.body: The wheels reacting to a fall came early, and the amount was the hard part. Too much proportional gain made it swing back and forth around its balance point and too little let it fall, so the derivative term went in to slow those fast corrections down. The integral term kept the motors pushing after the robot was already coming back upright, so we kept it small and clamped it in both firmwares. Values that worked on one chassis also didn't carry over to the next, so each one was tuned on its own, and the final Nano runs Kp 80, Ki 1.2, Kd 4.8 while the Pico runs Kp 75, Ki 2, Kd 3.

sections.heading: Finding the Balance Point
sections.body: Zero degrees was never the best balance point. Battery placement, the electronics, the wheel position and how the chassis went together all shifted it, so we tuned the target angle like another gain, and it ended up at -2 degrees on the Nano and -3 on the Pico. Moving weight around the chassis was part of that tuning too.

sections.heading: Motors That Wouldn't Start
sections.body: The motors needed a minimum power before they would move, so very small corrections didn't move the wheels at all. The fix was mapping the PID output into a PWM window that starts above that minimum, 150 to 255 on the Pico, while the Nano's floor steps up from 145 to 195 as the error grows and a 0.2 degree deadzone ignores tiny errors. The Pico was also weaker falling forward than backward, so its code boosts the error by 40% on that side and holds at least 185 PWM there. Both also cut the motors once the robot tips past about 35 degrees, so a bad gain can't keep the wheels spinning after a fall.

projects.title: Crab Crawler
projects.summary: We wanted a small walking robot students could understand and change without a complicated drivetrain.
projects.cardSummary: Crab Crawler is a four leg walking robot we built for the club to teach servo control and gait timing, the servo counterpart to the Self Balancing Robot. It went from a large Arduino Nano robot to two smaller ESP32 CAM versions that walk over Wi-Fi while streaming live video. The first was heavy enough to strip its servos, and the smaller one that replaced it cracked and had too little room inside for the wiring. The third version thickened the high stress areas and cleaned up the wiring, and it walks reliably.
projects.imageAlt: Three small ESP32 walking robots with servo-driven legs standing on a workbench.

overview.problem: The Self Balancing Robot teaches continuous feedback with DC motors, and we wanted something that taught positional servos moving through a timed sequence. A walker also put ESP32 programming, Wi-Fi control, a camera and a small display into one build simple enough to understand part by part.
overview.method: We built three versions with printed frames, starting with an Arduino Nano and moving to an ESP32 CAM with a PCA9685 servo driver and an OLED. The code runs the gait, the browser controls, the camera stream and the faces on the screen, and we changed the frame after each round of walking tests.
overview.result: The final crawler walks, takes commands over Wi-Fi from a browser, streams live video, and shows faces on its OLED. The project is complete, and the CAD for the compact and reinforced frames is in the repo.

sections.heading: Walking With Servos
sections.body: The crawler walks by stepping its legs through a timed sequence that shifts its weight and pushes against the floor. Small changes to servo position and timing made a noticeable difference in grip, so we tuned the printed legs and the sequence together. The PCA9685 board produces steady PWM for the leg servos so the ESP32 doesn't have to.

sections.heading: Wireless Control and Camera
sections.body: A phone or computer joins the robot's own network and sends a direction from the browser, the ESP32 picks the matching gait, and the camera streams video back, so you can drive it from its own point of view. The OLED faces show its status.

sections.heading: Version 1: Stripped Servos
sections.body: The first crawler used an Arduino Nano, a servo driver and a large printed body. It proved the walking sequence, but the body asked too much torque from the small servos, and some of them stripped under the load. Some parts were also too thin or put the load straight onto the servo mounts. So the second version shrank the frame around an ESP32 CAM, which took weight off the servos and added the Wi-Fi control and camera.

sections.heading: Version 2: Cracks and Crowded Wiring
sections.body: The smaller frame was thin enough that it cracked and broke under load during testing, and the wiring space inside was too tight, which made connections less reliable and parts harder to replace. The third version kept the ESP32 CAM, the servo driver and the four leg gait, thickened the frame where testing showed failures and cleaned up the wiring. That frame handled the load and walked more consistently, with fewer connection problems. The main lesson was that smaller isn't automatically stronger, since servo torque, linkage geometry, wall thickness, layer orientation and wire routing all decide whether a printed walker survives.

projects.title: TrainUI Mini
projects.summary: I wanted each club lesson to build toward something useful instead of students only running example programs.
projects.cardSummary: I built TrainUI Mini, a small e-paper train display based on TrainUI XL, as a project the City Tech club could build and learn from. It shows live MTA arrivals, service alerts, temperature and time on one ESP32 S3 board with a 2.13 inch e-paper screen, with no app, account or API key. The e-paper took the most work, since the picture flipped orientation between full and fast refreshes and the temperature would not update. Both are fixed and the board runs as a finished display.
projects.imageAlt: The TrainUI Mini e-paper train display standing on a desk.

overview.problem: TrainUI XL uses a Raspberry Pi Zero W and a 10.1 inch color screen, which made it too expensive and complicated to hand out as a club project, so I turned the same idea into a smaller and cheaper ESP32 build.
overview.method: I rebuilt the basic train and weather display around one Elecrow ESP32 S3 board with a built in 2.13 inch e-paper screen, so there is no separate computer, monitor, video cable, or most of the wiring. The code connects straight to the MTA and Open-Meteo, hosts its own setup page, and saves the settings on the board.
overview.result: It works as a finished train display and as a teaching project covering Arduino IDE, Wi-Fi, web requests, APIs, and e-paper. The Mini still keeps the main information I actually use from the larger version.

sections.heading: Live Data on One Board
sections.body: The ESP32 pulls the MTA's public realtime data, splits the chosen station's arrivals by direction, and shows the next three for each side. Arrivals refresh every minute, service alerts every five minutes, and the Open-Meteo weather every ten, with the clock synced over the internet.

sections.heading: Setup and Controls
sections.body: On first boot the board makes its own TrainUIMini network and serves a setup page where you enter your Wi-Fi, pick an NYC train and pick a station on that route, and the settings survive a restart or unplug. The buttons reopen setup or refresh, and pressing the dial switches to an offline sample mode with example arrivals and weather in the same layout. That mode keeps a club lesson working if the network or the MTA data is down.

sections.heading: Designing Around E-Paper
sections.body: E-paper can't redraw dozens of times a second like a normal screen, so the layout only holds information that changes every few minutes. Most updates use the faster partial refresh, and every tenth one is a full refresh to clear the ghosting.

sections.heading: The Picture Flipping Between Refreshes
sections.body: The screen's picture could change orientation between full and fast refreshes, because resetting the display controller also reset its scan direction and memory window. I fixed it by reapplying that setup after every controller reset and keeping the rotation in one place, so every refresh path draws the same way up.

sections.heading: Temperature and Off Center Badges
sections.body: The temperature wasn't updating because the code searched the whole weather response for its numbers instead of only the current conditions part of it. Now it reads only the current conditions, shows TEMP ERR when the request fails, and retries every minute until it works again. The route badge also looked off center, because the letters don't fill their character boxes evenly. The first fix centered on the width of the letters, and the final one centers on the pixels that are actually lit, so every route letter sits in the middle of its circle.

projects.title: AutoCAD I
projects.summary: I took AutoCAD I to learn proper 2D drafting, since my CAD experience up to then was 3D modeling in Fusion 360.
projects.cardSummary: AutoCAD I was my first drafting class, with weekly assignments, homework sets 1 through 8, quizzes, two midterms and a final project. The goal was turning the shape of a part into a drawing that's accurate, easy to read and ready to print. I already modeled in Fusion 360, so the geometry was straightforward and the new skill was drafting standards and drawing setup. By the end I was faster in AutoCAD and my drawings were cleaner and more consistent.
projects.imageAlt: An AutoCAD orthographic drawing showing top, front and right views of a bracket with dimensions and a completed title block.

overview.problem: Modeling a part and documenting it so someone else can make it are different skills, and the second one was the one I was missing.
overview.method: I practiced coordinates, dimensions, title blocks, layouts, and plotting, and every drawing ended as a plotted PDF.
overview.result: It got me used to keeping every sheet in the same format, and my drawings became easier to understand.

sections.heading: Drawing Precisely
sections.body: The early work was geometric construction, like tangent arcs, filter plates and practice layouts. I placed lines exactly with polar tracking, object snaps and direct distance entry instead of eyeballing them, and built repeated features with circular, polar and rectangular arrays.

sections.heading: Dimensions, Views and Title Blocks
sections.body: From there the drawings became multi view projections, like the Quiz 3 bracket with top, front and right views. I set up ANSI linear, aligned, radial and angular dimensions, scaled paper space viewports, and built my own title block template that fills in the drawing information automatically.

sections.heading: Quizzes, Midterms and the Final
sections.body: The quizzes were timed drawings, alongside two midterm drawing sets and a final. Everything was plotted with monochrome ANSI plot settings and standard title block revisions, and the archive ended at 95 files, with 41 drawings, 28 backup revisions and 23 plotted PDFs.

projects.title: AutoCAD II
projects.summary: I took AutoCAD II to get past the single sheets of AutoCAD I.
projects.cardSummary: AutoCAD II moved past single drawings into complete drawing sets, inch and metric dimensioning, and 3D solids, with the goal of documentation someone else could follow across several sheets. The assignments got too big to treat every sheet as its own file, and inch and metric drawings had to look the same even though their standards are different. Reusable title blocks and one format for every sheet fixed that, and the final was split across several connected drawings.
projects.imageAlt: A shaded 3D AutoCAD model of a coil spring on a dark background.

overview.problem: AutoCAD I was mostly about getting one drawing right. AutoCAD II was about keeping a whole set of drawings consistent, in two unit systems, and getting into 3D.
overview.method: I built reusable title blocks, worked with auxiliary and section views, and dimensioned drawings in both inch and metric. I modeled solids with sweeps, revolves, lofts, and Boolean operations.
overview.result: By the end, I was paying attention to the order of the sheets and the way someone else would read them, not only whether the geometry was correct. The archive ended up at 105 files.

sections.heading: Inch and Metric
sections.body: A lot of the class was dimensioning the same kind of part in both inch and metric. ANSI and ISO differ in how dimensions and tolerances are written, so the two kinds of drawing wouldn't match on their own. I set up inch and metric dimension styles for each standard and picked the right one before any dimension went on the drawing.

sections.heading: Too Many Sheets
sections.body: Once the sets got big, giving every sheet its own border and title block meant small differences started showing up between them, inch and metric alike. So I built the layout once, as title block templates and drawing borders in a TitleBlocks folder, and used them on every sheet so the 2D and 3D work all followed the same format. AutoCAD's .bak backups also became a revision history, with 44 of them kept next to 61 drawings.

sections.heading: 3D Solids and the Final
sections.body: The 3D work included a helical coil swept along a set pitch and diameter, and an isometric part dimensioned with linear, radius and diameter callouts. The final had multiple stages with sub assemblies 5A and 5B, and quiz 2 covered section views.

projects.title: Mastercam
projects.summary: I took Mastercam because drawing a part wasn't enough, and I wanted to know how to actually get a CNC machine to make it.
projects.cardSummary: In this class I programmed a three axis CNC mill through seven Mastercam tutorials and posted usable NC code. I already knew how to draw a part, but Mastercam made me decide how a mill would actually cut it. The new part was everything a CAD model doesn't say, like which cutter to use, where the stock begins and what order to cut the features in. I set up every job the same way, from stock and coordinate system to tools, feeds and simulation, and didn't post the NC file until the backplot made sense.
projects.imageAlt: A Mastercam simulation of a blue end mill cutting a pocket into a yellow and red block.
projects.motionImageAlt: Animated Mastercam toolpath simulation of an end mill machining a red block.

overview.problem: A CAD model does not tell the machine which cutter to use, where the stock begins, or what order the features should be cut in. Those choices were new to me.
overview.method: For each tutorial, I defined the stock, set the work origin, chose the tools, entered feeds and speeds, and built the operations one at a time. Backplot and simulation came before posting.
overview.result: The class gave me a process I could follow later on a real machine, and I did use it at the NYC FIRST STEM Center.

sections.heading: Setting Up Each Job
sections.body: Every tutorial started by bringing in the part geometry. The workpiece coordinate system is what tells the machine where zero is, and each tool, whether an endmill, ball mill or drill, got its own chip load, cutting speed and stepover.

sections.heading: Seven Tutorials
sections.body: Tutorial 1 was basic facing and contouring around a perimeter, and Tutorial 2 added pocketing around islands with staged roughing. Tutorial 3 had multi depth slotting and peck drilling, Tutorial 4 needed three setups with chamfering, and Tutorial 5 was circular interpolation and reaming a bore. Tutorial 6 moved into 3D surface roughing and finish contouring, and Tutorial 7 was a multi tool milling project.

sections.heading: Choices the CAD Doesn't Make
sections.body: Picking the cutter, deciding where the stock starts and choosing the order of features all change how long a part takes and whether a tool can even reach a feature. That's how a part that looks simple in CAD can still be slow or awkward to cut. Going through the same setup on every job meant each of those choices got made on purpose, and the simulation showed whether they worked before anything was posted.

sections.heading: Checking Before Posting
sections.body: The backplot and simulation were there to make sure the toolpath cleared the stock and nothing collided. The class produced 11 posted NC programs and 10 text post outputs from educational post processors, so none of them should go to a real machine without checking controller compatibility, tool stickout, stock size, work zero and clearance heights first.

sections.heading: On a Real Machine
sections.body: The tutorials were simulated, but during my internship on Roosevelt Island I used the same process for real, preparing workholding, setting up tooling, posting code and running three axis CNC mills to make robot parts.

media.label: Mastercam toolpath simulation
media.alt: Animated Mastercam toolpath simulation of an end mill machining a red block.

projects.title: MATLAB
projects.summary: I took MATLAB to learn the tool engineers use for calculations and data.
projects.cardSummary: This MATLAB class covered engineering calculations, data and plots through weekly labs, three exams and seven larger projects. The goal was turning an engineering problem into a program instead of solving it by hand every time. Coming from some Python, I had to get used to MATLAB working around matrices and engineering data. The projects were the most useful part, covering orbital motion, atmospheric models, GPU data, generated audio and demographic trends, and by the end I could rerun a calculation with different inputs and show the answer in a graph.
projects.imageAlt: A MATLAB horizontal bar chart of Steam hardware survey GPU market share by graphics card series.

overview.problem: My only programming before was some Python, and I had not used a language built around matrices and engineering data.
overview.method: I wrote scripts and reusable functions, imported data, and used plots to check whether the output actually matched the problem. The seven projects were done as a team of three, and they gave me much better practice than isolated equations did.
overview.result: I finished the class able to turn a longer calculation into a program and show the answer in a graph that another person could read.

sections.heading: Weekly Work and Exams
sections.body: The weekly classwork and textbook problems covered scripts, matrices, functions and plotting, from a sine wave plot to cone area, torus geometry and subplots, with three tests on top. By the end the folder had 88 .m scripts and functions along with published reports and figures.

sections.heading: The Seven Projects
sections.body: Project 1 charted Steam's April 2023 GPU survey as a horizontal bar chart, and Project 2 worked out how much bone mass astronauts lose in microgravity. Project 3 calculated atmospheric scale height at 700 K and 1600 K and the density at 250 km, and Project 4 found the angular size of the sun from Earth, 0.5457 degrees, and from Solar Probe Plus, 13.7634 degrees. Project 5 simulated an orbit, Project 6 generated sound with ADSR shaping and saved it as a .wav, and Project 7 imported a CSV of youth smoking data and looked at the trend with moving averages.

sections.heading: Thinking in Matrices
sections.body: The adjustment was writing code around whole arrays instead of looping through values one at a time like I would have in Python. Once each problem was set up that way, rerunning it with a different temperature or data set was just changing an input.

sections.heading: Checking With Plots
sections.body: Plotting became the way I checked my work as much as the way I presented it. If a curve or bar chart didn't look like the physical problem should, the code was wrong somewhere. Each project ended as a published report with the code, output and figures together.

projects.title: MECH 1101 Machine Shop
projects.summary: This class was my first time making a real part on manual shop tools.
projects.cardSummary: In MECH 1101 my group learned the manual shop tools by machining a blank metal plate into a finished part with four kinds of hole finishing, a square notch and filed edges, then inspecting it. Since a mistake can't be undone, planning the order of the work mattered as much as each cut. The part looked simple on the drawing, but four of the ten inspected features came out of tolerance, including the width, which came out 0.170 inches under size. The inspection showed how one early mistake carries into everything after it.
projects.imageAlt: A machined aluminium plate with milled steps and four drilled holes resting on a bench.

overview.problem: None of us could hide a bad setup with software. If a hole was misplaced or cut too large, the plate stayed that way.
overview.method: We marked the layout, drilled the starting holes, and then tapped, reamed, countersunk, or counterbored them as required. The notch and outside edges were finished by hand before inspection.
overview.result: Six of the ten inspected features passed and four failed. I became more comfortable using the shop tools, but the larger lesson was that a correct operation at the wrong time could still make the next step harder.

sections.heading: Layout
sections.body: On September 25 we started with the blank plate, coated it in blue Dykem layout dye, scribed the reference centerlines with a height gauge and center punched every hole location. Everything after that was cut to those marks, so the layout had to be right first.

sections.heading: Making the Holes
sections.body: On October 9 we drilled four pilot holes with a No. 5 bit and opened four outer holes to 1/4 in. and the center hole to 1/2 in. On October 30 we tapped the smallest hole to 1/4-20 UNC, reamed the center hole, countersunk the left hole and counterbored the right one.

sections.heading: Notch and Edges
sections.body: On November 6 we sanded the rough edge until the length measured 3.0 in. and cut a 1/2 in. square notch in the top. The next week we scribed 0.0625 in. corner details, and on November 20 we draw filed the corners down to the lines, deburred every edge and smoothed the bottom.

sections.heading: What the Inspection Found
sections.body: The length came out at exactly 3.000 in. and the notch at exactly 0.500 in., and the thickness was 0.369 in. against 0.368, inside its ±0.001. The width measured 2.830 in. against 3.000, and the sheet's reason is that too much was cut. The countersink diameter was 0.516 in., just over the 1/64 tolerance, with the note that the center of the hole was too far from the side of the part, and the Ø.500 hole came out 0.480 in. and the counterbore diameter came out too small. Inspection was the last step in the shop log, and the class records don't show any of the four being reworked afterward, so they stand as measured.

projects.title: Autodesk Inventor
projects.summary: I took Inventor to get better at the assembly and documentation side of CAD.
projects.cardSummary: This class used Autodesk Inventor for parametric parts, sheet metal, assemblies, drawings, exploded presentations and basic FEA, ending in a reusable bottle assembly. Single parts were familiar by then, so the goal was keeping a whole assembly organized, editable and documented. Every drawing and presentation points back to other model files, so a moved file or a changed early dimension could break what depended on it. Building from constrained dimensions and keeping assemblies next to their parts let me change an early dimension without breaking the rest.
projects.imageAlt: An Autodesk Inventor assembly drawing of a wheel assembly with numbered balloon callouts and a parts list.

overview.problem: Single parts were familiar by this point. Keeping a full assembly organized, editable, and documented was the part I still needed to practice.
overview.method: I built the models with dimensions and constraints, assembled them, and then made the drawings and exploded presentations from the same files. One assignment also used static stress analysis.
overview.result: I got much better at changing an early dimension without breaking everything that depended on it.

sections.heading: Parts and Sheet Metal
sections.body: The homework sets, 1 through 12, built up from constrained sketches and equations to extrudes, revolves, sweeps, lofts and threads. The sheet metal work covered K factor bend allowances, relief cuts, flanges and hems, with flat patterns generated for laser cutting and bending.

sections.heading: Assemblies, Drawings and FEA
sections.body: Assemblies used mate, flush, insert and tangent constraints, and exploded presentations showed how they come apart with a parts list. The drawings were associative, so section and detail views update with the model. Homework 12 was a plate stress study with a fine mesh, Von Mises stress contours and displacement plots, and another study loaded a bracket with 500 N on a fixed face.

sections.heading: Keeping the Files Linked
sections.body: Every drawing and presentation pointed back to another model, so file organization stopped being optional. If an assembly got separated from its part files it lost track of them, so I kept the .iam assemblies in the same folders as the .ipt parts they reference. Changing an early dimension could also break features and constraints that depended on it, so I built the parts from constrained sketches and dimensions that let an early change carry through to the rest.

sections.heading: The Mini Project and Final
sections.body: The mini project put four parts, an axle, base plate, bracket and wheel, into one assembly with PDF drawings. The final was a reusable bottle with a holder, a threaded lid and straw parts, an exploded presentation and my own drawing borders. By the end the archive had 109 parts, 20 assemblies and 4 presentations.

projects.title: Geopolymer Research
projects.summary: I wanted to find out if a normal consumer 3D printer could be turned into an open source machine for printing fly ash geopolymer.
projects.cardSummary: For undergraduate research at City Tech, I converted an Ender 5 Plus into a printer that pushes uncured geopolymer paste through a hose and nozzle instead of melting plastic. Our group was testing fly ash geopolymer as a lower carbon construction material, so the machine had to move a heavy, wet mixture at a steady rate. The paste kept coming out too stiff to pump or too runny to hold a layer, and the pump needed its own control that the printer's board couldn't give it. After a lot of mix testing and adding a second Klipper board that ties the pump to the toolhead, we printed multiple single layer shapes with a 65% fly ash mix.
projects.imageAlt: A CUNY City Tech Summer 2025 certificate of research achievement presented to Angelo Demetroulakos.

overview.problem: We were working with alkali activated fly ash as a possible lower carbon construction material, and one of the questions was whether it could be 3D printed at all. The objective on our poster was a geopolymer printer that could do multi layer printing with the same workflow as a normal FDM printer.
overview.method: I kept the Ender 5 Plus frame and motion system and redesigned the X axis carriage and toolhead around a custom extruder, fed by an external pump through a reinforced PTFE hose. A Raspberry Pi running Klipper controls the original board plus a second board for the pump. The rest of the group and I mixed and tested formulations until one held its shape and still flowed.
overview.result: We printed multiple single layer geometries, which showed the modified printer could handle the high viscosity paste. Multi layer printing, the original objective, isn't there yet. The CO2 adsorption side ended without data and has to start over.

sections.heading: Changing the Printer
sections.body: The redesigned mount moved the extruder and the CR Touch probe so the carriage could hold more than one extruder and the extruder and tube were easy to reach. The printer hosts its own control page over local Wi-Fi and runs without internet, which matters for the lunar construction side of the research. G-code comes from CAD models sliced in PrusaSlicer with profiles set up for paste and no retraction.

sections.heading: Finding a Mix That Prints
sections.body: Filament is solid until the hot end melts it, but our geopolymer started as a thick paste that had to move under pressure and then stop flowing once it reached the bed. Too stiff and the pump struggled, and too wet and the layer flattened. To find something in between we changed the amounts of fly ash, potassium silicate, potassium hydroxide and water between tests, and some trials added 5% or 10% sand or used finer fly ash. Each mix was judged by how it traveled through the hose, how smoothly it extruded, and how well it held its shape and bonded between layers, aiming for something like clay. The best results came from 65% fly ash, 17.5% potassium silicate and 17.5% potassium hydroxide, with water added a little at a time until the viscosity was right.

sections.heading: Incomplete Klipper Config
sections.body: The Raspberry Pi was first connected to the printer's BTT SKR E3 Mini mainboard, which came with Klipper already flashed but with incomplete configuration files, so the printer setup had to be filled in before anything else worked. The config files in the repo now cover the kinematics, axis limits, CR Touch probing and pinouts, plus macros for homing, bed mesh, priming and cancelling a print.

sections.heading: A Pump With No Controller
sections.body: The pump needed its own motor control. The only other way to run it was a separate Arduino that wouldn't follow the printer's G-code, and the older config ran the pump as its own second extruder, apart from the toolhead's moves. I added a second board, a BTT Octopus, so Klipper runs the pump alongside the SKR E3 and no Arduino is needed. The pump is now an extruder_stepper tied to the toolhead extruder, so both follow the same extrusion moves in the G-code, and that synchronized control gave consistent flow on the single layer prints.

sections.heading: The CO2 Samples
sections.body: For the carbon dioxide side, the materials team mixed fly ash geopolymer with 0 to 15 wt% hydrotalcite and surfactant, cured the samples at 90 °C for 5 hours, and heated some of them again at 300 °C. The idea was more pore surface for the gas to adsorb onto while keeping enough strength for structural or printed parts. The samples came out too porous after oven curing to be usable, so there's no test data and that study has to start over. The plan on the poster is to keep characterizing new samples with SEM, STA, BET and tensile testing to see if they can do as well as concrete or better.

sections.heading: What's Next for the Printer
sections.body: The next steps from the poster are a stable mount for the pump extruder to make it more precise, a partial enclosure that also deals with cooling the electronics, and a local heater that cures the geopolymer while it prints so there's less post processing.

projects.title: City Tech & NYU Summer Camp
projects.summary: I joined to get hands on time with the materials labs, machines and inspection equipment that I'd mostly only seen from the CAD side.
projects.cardSummary: I completed a month long advanced materials and manufacturing program split between City Tech and NYU Tandon, from May 27 to June 26, 2025. It was meant to show the whole path a part takes, with a different side of manufacturing almost every week. I examined materials under microscopes, programmed a CNC mill, made parts with different 3D printing processes, and checked finished dimensions on a CMM. It ended with a capstone presentation on how an idea moves through design, manufacturing, inspection and product development.
projects.imageAlt: An NSF ATE Summer Training Camp certificate of completion from City Tech and NYU presented to Angelo Demetroulakos.

overview.problem: Most of my experience before this was designing parts on a computer and 3D printing them. The program covered the parts I hadn't done much of, like looking at a material's structure, machining, measuring a finished part against its tolerances, and what it takes to bring a product to market.
overview.method: Each block of a few days focused on one area, from materials characterization through CNC milling, SolidWorks, three kinds of 3D printing, commercialization, medical devices and GD&T on a CMM. I documented each week with photos, notes, CAD files, part files and a recap video.
overview.result: I finished the program with a machined aluminum part, a capstone presentation, and five weekly recap videos. The biggest thing I took from it was seeing how the manufacturing process changes what can actually be made.

sections.heading: Learning the Material First
sections.body: The first two days, May 27 and 28, covered materials characterization, optical metallography and mounting specimens. I examined microstructures, grain boundaries, fracture surfaces and elemental composition maps with optical microscopy and SEM/EDS. It showed me how much a surface that looks ordinary without magnification can reveal about a material or a failure.

sections.heading: Three Ways to Print a Part
sections.body: June 9 and 10 were SolidWorks, and June 11 and 12 were powder bed fusion, SLA resin and composite FDM printing. Side by side, the differences in surface finish, accuracy and material choice were much clearer. A separate session on May 29 covered cybersecurity and intellectual property in additive manufacturing.

sections.heading: Making and Checking a CNC Part
sections.body: From June 2 to 5 I programmed facing, pocketing, contouring and engraving on a three axis CNC vertical mill and machined a camp part from aluminum, which connected CAD geometry to the actual sequence of operations, tool movement and setup. From June 23 to 25 I checked part features against their intended dimensions with GD&T and a coordinate measuring machine. Tolerances felt a lot more practical once I could see how they were verified on a real component.

sections.heading: Engineering Beyond Manufacturing
sections.body: June 16 and 17 covered technology commercialization, innovation and pitching, and June 18 was biocompatible materials and medical device development with 3D printing. Those sessions showed how cost, regulations, intellectual property and whether a product can realistically be manufactured all affect design decisions.

sections.heading: Capstone and Documentation
sections.body: On June 26 we gave our capstone presentations at a symposium with industry experts. Because I'd kept notes, files and recap videos all month, I had a record of the work and not only the final part.

projects.title: STEM Research Academy Near Peer Mentor
projects.summary: The program had two high school students learn every part of a robot by building one themselves instead of from a kit, and I was there to guide them through it.
projects.cardSummary: For six weeks I was one of four college mentors guiding two high school students from small training robots to 3TSahur, a Raspberry Pi mecanum robot with a camera, browser controls and a servo ramp. I mentored mostly on the electronics, Linux and programming. The hardest parts were the ramp, where the PCA9685 servo board didn't work and the Pi's software PWM made the servos jitter, and motor directions that had to be worked out on the real robot. We moved the servos to direct GPIO timed by pigpio and settled on a mecanum mix checked by testing every direction.
projects.imageAlt: A STEM Research Academy certificate of completion presented to Angelo Demetroulakos.

overview.problem: The STEM Research Academy Robot Lab gave two high school students six weeks to work through CAD, fabrication, power, wiring, motors, cameras, networking and Python on one robot. They needed someone who could help with the electrical and software side without just doing it for them.
overview.method: The first three weeks were smaller robots and single skills, and the last three went into 3TSahur. I mentored mostly on microcontrollers, Raspberry Pi setup, Linux, wiring, firmware and debugging, and pitched in on CAD and 3D printing when the robot needed custom parts.
overview.result: 3TSahur drives in every direction, streams its camera to a browser and opens and closes its ramp, and the team presented it with posters and their completion certificates. Mentoring was different from building a robot for myself because I had to explain why something worked instead of just fixing it.

sections.heading: Building Skills in Stages
sections.body: The smaller builds, including two ESP32-S3 and ESP32-CAM robots that make their own Wi-Fi networks, let the students learn motors, controllers, wiring and code without troubleshooting a whole robot at once. When something failed, I tried not to give them the answer right away. We worked out whether the problem was the mechanical build, the wiring, the firmware or the software, and I showed them how to trace wiring and isolate a fault instead of swapping parts at random.

sections.heading: Building 3TSahur
sections.body: 3TSahur is a Raspberry Pi 4 with four mecanum wheels on two dual H-bridge drivers, a Logitech USB camera, and a two servo ramp meant to carry the smaller robots from earlier in the program. The 12 V motor power is kept separate from the Pi's 5 V logic, with a fuse, a common ground, a buck converter for the servos and custom PCBs. The students built the mechanical side with CAD, 3D printing, the bandsaw, drilling and manual milling, and I made printed parts with them that fit around the electronics and drivetrain.

sections.heading: The Ramp Servos
sections.body: The ramp was supposed to run off a PCA9685 servo board over I2C, but the board didn't work, so we moved both servos onto the Pi's GPIO12 and GPIO18 pins. The Pi's normal software PWM isn't steady, so the idle servos hunted and jittered. The first fix held each position for 0.6 seconds and then cut the signal. The fix that stuck was the pigpio daemon, which times continuous pulses independently of the Linux process, so both servos now hold the ramp at 0° closed or 120° open without jitter.

sections.heading: Getting the Wheels to Agree
sections.body: The motor directions didn't match what the wiring said they should. Physical testing first showed the two left motors had opposite polarity, and the mapping changed again the next day before it settled. Instead of moving wires, we fixed the directions in software and put the mix that matched the real robot in mixer.py, with a test that checks every direction at the actual GPIO pins. The final setup inverts forward and back for the whole chassis, keeps strafing as it was, and turns the robot on the spot with Q and E at 75% on all four wheels.

sections.heading: After the Program
sections.body: After the program I moved 3TSahur onto MotionModule, so it now runs a Driver Station at 3tsahur.local, falls back to its own hotspot after 30 seconds without Wi-Fi, stops the motors if commands stop for 300 ms, and takes code updates over Wi-Fi.

projects.title: NYC FIRST STEM Center Summer Internship
projects.summary: The internship let me take one mechanical system, a swerve pod for brand new FIRST hardware, from the first CAD all the way to machined parts on a driving robot.
projects.cardSummary: During a six week internship at the NYC FIRST STEM Center, I designed the drivetrain for a robot built around the new A301 motors and Systemcore. I started with a one week mecanum chassis to get the early hardware moving, then designed custom swerve pods and revised them through five versions. When I CNC machined the V3 pods, the main bearing hole came out too tight and the pods didn't rotate smoothly. I still finished a four pod robot driving on eight A301 motors, and corrected the bearing fit in a V3.1 design toleranced for CNC.
projects.imageAlt: A NYC FIRST certificate of completion for the STEM Center at Cornell Tech summer internship, presented to Angelo Demetroulakos.

overview.problem: Systemcore, Motioncore and the A301 motors were new, early hardware, and the STEM Center needed a robot to test them on. My job was the mechanical side of that robot. It was also my first real time running CNC mills for robot parts instead of simulating toolpaths in class.
overview.method: Week one was a simple mecanum chassis to bring up Systemcore, Motioncore, the A301s and the 18 volt battery pack. Weeks two through four went into designing, printing and revising the swerve pod, weeks four and five tested a two pod chassis on casters, and in week six four machined pods went onto the final robot.
overview.result: The final robot drives on four V3 pods with eight A301 motors, one drive and one steering motor in each, with the old mecanum wheels underneath left as passive support. It worked, but V3 isn't the last version. V3.1 fixes the bearing hole in CAD, and the ratchet still has to be added.

sections.heading: Starting With a Test Platform
sections.body: The mecanum chassis got us something running quickly, and it showed things CAD alone wouldn't, like how much room the electronics needed, where wiring should go and how the new hardware behaved moving a robot. In the last week that chassis was cut from metal so the nose drawer could mount above it.

sections.heading: Five Versions of the Pod
sections.body: I printed the early versions so I could change parts quickly without wasting machining time, and each test exposed packaging, steering, gearing or assembly problems. V1 steered through a 16T to 36T pulley, and V2 replaced the belt with a center shaft bolted straight to the pod and a fully geared drive into a 2.8:1 Axon bevel, reworked in V2.25 and V2.5. V3 put the steering motor directly at the center of rotation, made the pod slimmer, and switched to a 3.1:1 offset bevel. Its wheel became a print in place part with a TPU tread, easier to manage than the old bolted tread and with less friction than rubber on FTC mats.

sections.heading: Two Pods First
sections.body: The two pod chassis on casters was for working out steering and diagonal driving before building four pods. Another intern focused on the software, with test modes for calibrating the pods with their absolute encoders and checking drive and steering direction. A301 position control through REVLib turned the encoder readings into impossible values and threw Sensor Faults, and that wasn't solved during the internship. The team stopped using the position control test because the feedback couldn't be trusted, and wrote the fault up as an issue report with the firmware and library versions.

sections.heading: The V3 Bearing Problem
sections.body: V3 was the first version I CNC machined instead of printing. During assembly the main bearing hole turned out too tight, which squeezed the bearing and kept the pod from rotating smoothly. I fixed it in V3.1, which is toleranced specifically for CNC, with a bearing hole that gives the bearing room to seat and the pod room to turn and the same drivetrain layout as V3. That fix is in the CAD, and the pods on the robot are still the machined V3s.

sections.heading: The Ratchet and the Final Robot
sections.body: The ratchet couldn't be ordered in time, so the physical pods run without it, but its mounting holes are already in the module so it can go in later without a redesign. The final robot has no casters, and its eight A301 motors run through Systemcore and Motioncore. I also finished training on the center's CNC machines, laser cutter and 3D printers, and by the end I was making the final parts on them.

projects.title: A301 Chassis Swechanum
projects.summary: We needed one complete robot to test the new A301 motors on.
projects.cardSummary: Swechanum is a test robot I designed and built during my internship that combines a mecanum chassis and four A301 swerve modules on one frame. It gave the team a complete robot for testing the new A301 motors, and students can learn mecanum and then move up to swerve on the same robot. We only had eight A301 motors, and the gearbox cartridges were 500 RPM instead of the 2,000 RPM the drivetrain was designed for. All eight motors went into the swerve modules, so the mecanum wheels roll free for now, and the robot drives and steers on all four pods at a lower speed than planned.
projects.programSummary: I built Swechanum during my six week internship at the NYC FIRST STEM Center at Cornell Tech. I handled the mechanical design, manufacturing, and assembly while another intern worked on the software.
projects.imageAlt: CAD render of the A301 Swechanum chassis seen from the front.

overview.problem: The robot had to test the A301 motors with Systemcore and Motioncore. Keeping the original mecanum system also gave new students a simpler drivetrain to learn before steering calibration and swerve control.
overview.method: I designed the chassis and swerve system, iterated through printed prototypes, created the CAM, machined the final parts, and assembled the robot. Another intern wrote the software, and my supervisor and coworkers reviewed each mechanical revision.
overview.result: The goal was a robot that could run both drivetrains, and it got partway there. Swerve drives and steers on all four pods, and the mecanum side will be powered once more motors are available.

sections.heading: Two Drivetrains on One Platform
sections.body: Students start with fixed mecanum wheels to learn individual motor control and omnidirectional movement, then move to modules where each wheel also controls its own steering angle. I left the mechanisms exposed so students can watch the gears, motors, and steering while connecting them to the encoders, IMUs, and code.

sections.heading: Building the Final Chassis
sections.body: The test structure started in plywood because it was fast to make and change. Once the dimensions and layout were set, I rebuilt it in goBILDA metal channel, plates, and hardware and mounted the four swerve modules. Systemcore and Motioncore on the robot control all eight A301 motors.

sections.heading: Going from Two Pods to Four
sections.body: In weeks 4 and 5 the robot ran on two powered swerve pods with casters holding up the rest, which let us develop the steering and an early diagonal two pod drive while I built the other pods. In week 6 the casters came off and all four V3 pods went on.

sections.heading: Only Eight Motors
sections.body: Powering both drivetrains takes twelve A301 motors, and we had eight. Each swerve pod needs a drive and a steering motor, so all eight went into the swerve modules and the mecanum wheels became passive supports. That isn't fixed yet, and the mecanum side will be powered once we get more motors.

sections.heading: The Slower Cartridges
sections.body: The drivetrain was designed for 2,000 RPM A301 gearbox cartridges, but the alpha testing hardware came with 500 RPM cartridges. That isn't fixed yet either, so the robot is much slower than intended, but all four modules could still be tested steering and driving together.

sections.heading: How It Runs Now
sections.body: The robot drives entirely on the four swerve pods in the final four module drive mode. The code includes the calibration and direction tests for aligning each pod's absolute encoder and checking every motor. The CAD and code are open source, including the earlier two pod CAD.

projects.title: A301 Swerve Module
projects.summary: I designed this from scratch during my internship as the Swechanum robot's swerve drive.
projects.cardSummary: This is a two motor A301 swerve module I designed for the Swechanum robot, where one motor drives the wheel and the other steers the whole pod. The robot needed a compact module that could drive and steer on its own and stay open enough for students to see how it works. In four weeks it went from printed prototypes with belt steering to four machined pods with the steering motor on the rotation axis and a 3.1:1 drive. The first machined version had a bearing bore too tight to turn smoothly, so I corrected the tolerance in V3.1 without changing anything else in the layout.
projects.programSummary: I developed the module during my six week internship at the NYC FIRST STEM Center at Cornell Tech as the main drivetrain for the Swechanum robot.
projects.imageAlt: CAD render of four A301 swerve pods installed on a test chassis.

overview.problem: Each pod had to drive and steer independently on two A301 motors while staying compact. Because the robot was also for teaching, the mechanism had to stay open and easy to follow.
overview.method: I iterated through V1, V2, V2.25, V2.5, and V3 between weeks 2 and 4, 3D printing the early versions before machining the final design. Each version changed either how the pod steered or how power reached the wheel.
overview.result: Four V3 modules were machined and tested on the complete robot, which was the goal. V3.1 corrects the one fit problem found in V3 in the CAD, and the repository keeps every version from V1 to V3.

sections.heading: Prototyping Before CNC
sections.body: Printing the early versions let me check clearances, assembly order, gear placement, and overall size while parts were cheap and fast to replace.

sections.heading: Drive Layout
sections.body: The drive motor sits above the rotating part and sends power through two 1:1 spur stages, 64T to 64T and 20T to 20T, to a 3.1:1 offset bevel at the wheel, which does the full reduction. V2 and V2.5 used a 2.8:1 Axon bevel, and V3 made the pod slimmer with the 3.1:1 offset bevel set.

sections.heading: Wheel and Tread
sections.body: The wheel's rigid body and TPU tread print together on a multimaterial printer, which is easier to manage than the earlier bolted tread. On FTC mats the TPU grips well without grabbing the mat as hard as rubber.

sections.heading: Simplifying the Steering
sections.body: V1 steered through a belt and pulleys, and the extra belt, pulleys, and tensioning hardware added complexity without enough benefit. V2 switched to a direct bolted center shaft, and by V3 the steering motor sits directly over the center of rotation and turns the lower assembly one to one.

sections.heading: The V3 Bearing Problem
sections.body: V3 was the first CNC machined version, and its fits hadn't been toleranced for machining. The main bearing bore came out too tight, and pressing the bearing in squeezed it enough that the pod wouldn't rotate smoothly. In the V3.1 CAD I kept the V3 package and drivetrain and only changed the bearing hole fit, so the bearing has the clearance to seat correctly and the pod can turn smoothly. The four pods on the robot are the machined V3s, and the ratchet isn't on them yet because it couldn't be ordered in time, though its mounting holes are already in place.

projects.title: STEM Research Academy Robot Lab
projects.summary: This program took two students all the way to a robot they designed, wired, and programmed themselves.
projects.cardSummary: I mentored two high school students through six weeks of robotics, starting with small training robots and ending with 3TSahur, a Raspberry Pi mecanum robot with a camera and a servo ramp. Small projects first let them learn electronics, Linux, and code before debugging a full robot. The hardest problem in the final build was the ramp, because the planned servo driver board didn't work and running the servos straight from the Pi made them twitch while holding still. We fixed it by driving both servos from the Pi's GPIO with pigpio timing the pulses, and the robot finished with its own Wi-Fi and browser controls.
projects.programSummary: I worked as a near-peer mentor for two high school students during the six week STEM Research Academy program, helping them build up the skills needed to complete their own robot.
projects.imageAlt: The completed robot built by the STEM Research Academy students.

overview.problem: The students had limited robotics experience, so we didn't start them on a large robot. Smaller projects let them learn the basics and make mistakes without troubleshooting a whole system at once.
overview.method: I taught electronics and software, covering wiring, power, microcontrollers, firmware, signals, Linux, and Raspberry Pi setup. I also helped with CAD and 3D printing when the projects needed mechanical parts.
overview.result: The students built the final robot in the second half of the program, finished it, and presented it with their research at the end. Afterward I ported it to MotionModule, the club's Raspberry Pi robot runtime.

sections.heading: Power, Wiring, and Signals
sections.body: I taught how the robot's power was split between 12 volts for the motors and 5 volts from buck converters for the Pi and servos. We covered common grounds, fuses, motor drivers, connectors, soldering, and checking connections before power, then PWM, USB communication, firmware flashing, and how commands move between devices.

sections.heading: Learning Linux
sections.body: The Raspberry Pi introduced them to a full operating system instead of only flashing a microcontroller. I walked them through Raspberry Pi OS, basic Linux, hardware connections, starting the robot software, and what happens at boot.

sections.heading: Building 3TSahur
sections.body: The final robot has a Raspberry Pi 4, four mecanum wheels on two H-bridge drivers, a Logitech C270 camera, and a two servo ramp. The students programmed the mecanum drive and ramp servos, and the mentors guided the networking and browser interface. The ramp carries two minibots from the first three weeks, built on ESP32 S3 and ESP32 CAM boards.

sections.heading: Wheels Going the Wrong Way
sections.body: In the first test with the wheels raised, some motors spun backwards for where they were mounted. We swapped those motors' forward and reverse pins in software, ending with the two rear motors flipped. I had the students narrow problems down to power, wiring, firmware, code, or mechanical before changing anything.

sections.heading: The Servo Driver That Didn't Work
sections.body: The planned Adafruit PCA9685 servo driver didn't work on the robot, so we moved both ramp servos straight onto the Pi's GPIO12 and GPIO18. Powering them from the Pi's 5 V pins then risked undervoltage resets from servo current spikes, so the servos now run from a buck converter set to 5.0 V with its ground tied to the Pi.

sections.heading: Twitching Ramp Servos
sections.body: Linux software PWM has timing jitter, which made the servos hunt while holding still. Our first fix cut the signal 0.6 seconds after each move, which stopped the hunting, but then the ramp wouldn't hold against anything pushing on it. We switched to pigpio, which times the pulses outside the dashboard's process and keeps sending them, so both servos now hold their position steadily.

sections.heading: Moving to MotionModule
sections.body: After the program I moved 3TSahur onto MotionModule, so one command over SSH sets everything up. The Pi joins saved Wi-Fi or starts its own hotspot, drives from a keyboard, controller, or phone with the camera streaming, and stops the motors if commands stop.

projects.title: A301 Mecanum Chassis
projects.summary: We needed something simple that could drive the new A301 hardware right away.
projects.cardSummary: This plywood mecanum chassis was the first robot of my internship, which I built in one day so the team could test the new A301 motors and Systemcore hardware before the swerve modules were ready. It later stayed on as the simpler drivetrain students learn on before swerve. The layout kept changing as we learned how much room the electronics and wiring really needed. I reworked the layout, designed each motor and wheel assembly to pivot out for service, and in the final week rebuilt the structure in metal to carry the nose drawer.
projects.programSummary: I built the chassis during my six week internship at the NYC FIRST STEM Center at Cornell Tech as the first development platform for the larger Swechanum project.
projects.imageAlt: The first plywood A301 mecanum chassis prototype with its wheels fitted.

overview.problem: The A301 motors, Systemcore and Motioncore electronics, 18 volt battery, and sensors were all new to us, and the swerve modules were weeks away. Mecanum gives omnidirectional movement with no steering mechanism, so it was the fastest way to a test robot.
overview.method: I designed and built the first chassis in plywood, tested component layouts, added pivoting motor assemblies, and later manufactured the final structure in metal. I was finishing my training on the STEM Center's CNC machines, laser cutter, and 3D printers at the same time and put them to work on these parts.
overview.result: It met its goal. It served as the hardware test platform for the first part of the internship and became the lower half of Swechanum, where students can learn on it before moving to swerve. Its wheels roll free for now because we only had eight A301 motors.

sections.heading: A One Day Prototype
sections.body: Plywood let me build a complete chassis on the first day, so the team could start testing motors, electronics, software, and component placement immediately.

sections.heading: Finding Room for Everything
sections.body: Once the motors, battery, and control hardware were mounted together, the electronics and wiring needed more room than the first layout allowed. I kept revising the plywood version as the rest of the robot developed instead of locking the design in early.

sections.heading: Designing Around Maintenance
sections.body: Working on a motor or cartridge shouldn't mean taking the drivetrain apart, so each motor and wheel assembly pivots outward from the chassis. That gives direct access to the A301 motor, gearbox cartridge, wiring, wheel, and locking collar.

sections.heading: From Plywood to Metal
sections.body: Once the key dimensions and mounting points were set, I moved the design to metal. In the final week the chassis was cut and assembled in metal, giving the nose drawer a strong base to mount above the drivetrain.

projects.title: Glowlings
projects.summary: I wanted a small character I could carry that reacts to being held and touched instead of looping one animation.
projects.cardSummary: Star is a small ESP32-S3 keychain with a round touch display and animated eyes, the first character in my Glowlings project. The goal was a character that reacts to being held, so the eyes follow a finger, tilt with the board, get dizzy when shaken, and turn green while charging. The hard part was charging, since the board can only read battery voltage and Star kept its green charging eyes after being unplugged near full. I changed the detector to track the smoothed peak voltage and wait for a sustained drop, but voltage alone still misses some unplugs and can't see a cable already connected at startup.
projects.imageAlt: Star, a small round electronic keychain, showing green animated eyes while connected to USB power.
projects.motionImageAlt: Star looking around and tilting its eyes while green charging bubbles rise through them.

overview.problem: It had to be small enough for a keychain and run entirely on the device, with no Wi-Fi, phone, or cloud connection.
overview.method: I built Star on a Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-1.28 board and programmed the face to render on the device. I connected the eye animations to touch gestures, the motion sensor, and battery readings, and wrote desktop tests and a three hour simulated soak to check behavior before flashing.
overview.result: Star reacts to touch, motion, and charging, with bubbles while charging and tired red eyes when the battery is low. Charging detection is still a guess from voltage, so some cable changes are missed, and the repo documents those limits. Star is the first Glowling, and the desk buddies are still to come.

sections.heading: Starting with Star
sections.body: Star was inspired by CREATURE's Starboy. Frames go to the screen by DMA in 32 KB chunks while the CPU sleeps, capped at 20 FPS.

sections.heading: Touch and Movement
sections.body: A finger draws the gaze around the screen, swipes change the expression to sad, shy, or happy, and quick taps make it angry. Tilting moves the eyes, and a sustained shake brings up spiral pupils. It sleeps after a short idle, and a tap and hold toggles an always on mode that drops to 10 FPS when left alone.

sections.heading: Keeping the Eyes Centered
sections.body: Moving around while holding it made the gaze drift. Now each wake centers the gaze, it gently recenters while held steady, and a double tap sets the current pose as straight ahead. The soak test also found an eye could reach the bezel when several effects stacked, so any overflow now moves the eye inward.

sections.heading: Green Eyes After Unplugging
sections.body: The board can only read battery voltage on GPIO1, since neither the charger's status pin nor USB power is wired to the ESP32. Unplugging near full left the eyes green because the detector's reference followed the voltage down, and in testing unplugging only dropped it from about 4.148 V to 4.133 V. I changed the reference to the smoothed peak, let it fall only 1.8 mV a minute, and call it unplugged after a 15 mV sag held for one second.

sections.heading: What Voltage Can't Tell
sections.body: A 10 mV threshold caught unplugging faster but falsely triggered 2.5 seconds after a normal load step in a replay, so I never flashed it. Charging is capped at 99% since voltage alone can't prove a full battery. A near full unplug can still be missed, and a cable already connected at startup gives no rise to detect, so neither is fully fixed. The docs say that needs a hardware signal the board doesn't give the ESP32.

projects.title: Torque
projects.summary: I made Torque so a team could do all of their robot work in one free app, even before the robot exists.
projects.cardSummary: Torque is a free app I built so an FTC team can drive, set up, and test their robot in one place. It has its own Driver Station, a simulator for planning autonomous before the robot exists, and step by step tuning from real Control Hub readings. The hard part was making simulated runs match the real robot, since early exports assumed every Control Hub was mounted the same way and the example code had never been compiled against the real FTC SDK. Now setup records how the hub is mounted and every export is compiled against FTC SDK 12.0.0 and Pedro Pathing 3.0.2.
projects.imageAlt: Nox, a competition robot, driving its autonomous on the BIOBUZZ field in Torque's simulator.
projects.motionImageAlt: Nox driving the first cycle of its autonomous on the BIOBUZZ field in Torque's simulator, firing a volley of game pieces into the goal for its first 20 points.

overview.problem: Driving, checking wiring, and testing autonomous usually take several separate programs, and an autonomous route can't be tested until the robot is built.
overview.method: I built Torque as a desktop app with a Driver Station, a physics simulator, and a calibration tool. It started on October 17, 2026 as a Driver Station, and the simulator and calibration grew from there. The simulator runs on DSIM, and routes export as OnBot Java, TeamCode, or Pedro Pathing 3 code or upload straight to a Control Hub over Wi-Fi.
overview.result: Torque is released and working, and I'm still adding to it. It installs with one command on Windows and also runs on a Steam Deck and Apple Silicon Macs. The animation on this card is our team robot Nox running a three cycle autonomous in the simulator.

sections.heading: Driving
sections.body: The Driver Station runs op modes, shows telemetry, and supports two gamepads over Wi-Fi or USB with a Control Hub or Robot Controller phone. It also drives robots outside FTC, opening the web page of an ESP32, Raspberry Pi, or MotionModule robot and passing the gamepad through. A test screen shows every input and measures stick drift.

sections.heading: Simulator
sections.body: Teams set the robot's size, drivetrain, motors, sensors, and mechanisms like intakes, shooters, and turrets, or import their own CAD. Paths are clicked or drawn on the BIOBUZZ field, and Torque keeps the whole robot clear of obstacles. Runs can be scrubbed on a timeline, graphed for speed and heading, checked for pieces picked up and scored, and cut into an MP4.

sections.heading: Calibration
sections.body: Torque reads every motor, servo, and sensor the Control Hub reports and maps them into the robot setup with one button. Each mechanism is tuned in order, direction, units, zero, range, then control, and each step must pass before the next opens so one bad reading can't spoil the rest. The tuned values export as a Java file, and it can also program Axon servos.

sections.heading: When the Code Didn't Match the Robot
sections.body: The simulator is only useful if its exported code behaves the same on a real robot, and some didn't. Every export assumed the Control Hub was mounted logo up with the USB ports forward, so any other mounting would turn the robot wrong. I added two settings to Setup for which way the hub's logo and its USB ports face, and every OnBot, TeamCode, and Pedro export now writes them into the hub's mounting.

sections.heading: Code That Had Never Been Compiled
sections.body: The example mechanism code had never been compiled against the real FTC SDK. I added a check that downloads FTC SDK 12.0.0 and Pedro Pathing 3.0.2 and compiles every export against them, the examples' mechanism code included.

sections.heading: The Turret That Never Fired
sections.body: A servo turret timed itself from the last change, and pose noise kept pushing that time back, so it never fired. I changed it to track the turret's angle instead, to within 2 degrees.

sections.heading: Choppy Playback
sections.body: Runs looked choppy because new frames only reached the page 21 to 24 times a second, held back by how often Windows wakes the engine's timer. I changed when frames are sent and had the robot, its mechanisms, and the pieces glide between frames at the display's rate, which took the 3D view from 28 to 55 frames a second. Big CAD robots made it worse, so the 3D view now draws a lighter copy of a heavy CAD body, about 390 thousand triangles instead of 2.18 million.

sections.heading: Confusing Results
sections.body: The results disagreed with each other. One run said it finished in 10.53 s, the analysis box said 14.6 s because it was really counting time recorded, and the clock read 0:16, and a wall contact was counted just because the robot started against the wall. I replaced that box with one run report built from the recorded frames, which says whether the route worked, only counts contacts after the robot leaves its start, and points to the path to fix next.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.body: Torque isn't a safety system and the Driver Station isn't certified for competition. The physics engine is licensed for noncommercial use only, so the full release is free for uses like team practice.
