projects.title: MotionModule
projects.summary: I wanted anyone to be able to build their own robot controller from open code, a wiring guide, a parts list, and CAD.
projects.cardSummary: MotionModule is an open source Raspberry Pi robot controller I designed to replace a REV Control Hub and Expansion Hub with one box anyone can build, running eight brushed motors, sixteen servos, and an IMU from a browser dashboard. The REV hubs are expensive and closed, so I wanted one built from regular parts that works on any robot. In testing, the IMU autonomous had its heading correction backwards, which my simulation had hidden, and then it overshot its turns. I flipped the sign and added a PID that slows each approach, and my mecanum test robot now completes all four turns in 3.4 to 3.7 seconds.
projects.imageAlt: The MotionModule enclosure mounted on a mecanum test robot.

overview.problem: The REV hubs cost a lot and can't be opened up to see how they work. The controller had to be built from regular parts and run any robot, whether mecanum, tank, or walking.
overview.method: I wired a Raspberry Pi 5 to four dual H-bridge boards, a PCA9685 servo board, and an MPU6500 IMU, and designed a printed enclosure and a separate battery box. I wrote the software for GPIO, I2C, safety, Wi-Fi, and the dashboard, so each robot only needs its own Python folder.
overview.result: It works and is still in development. It runs my mecanum test robot in teleop and in an IMU autonomous that turns to 90, 180, 270, and back to the start. There is also a Mini version with two motor drivers and a demo that runs the real dashboard with a simulated robot.

sections.heading: Hardware
sections.body: The full build has eight motor outputs and sixteen servo outputs. One 12 V battery powers everything, stepped down to 5 V for the Pi and to a separate servo rail. The battery box fits both REV Slim and goBILDA 12 V NiMH batteries and hides the buck converters and power distribution.

sections.heading: Dashboard and Driver Station
sections.body: The dashboard opens at motionmodule.local on the same Wi-Fi, and the robot makes its own hotspot if it can't find a saved network. It shows live motor power, servo commands, temperature, and network status, plus an offline wiring map, parts list, and motor and servo tests. The Driver Station runs the robot's own Teleop and Autonomous code from a keyboard, controller, or phone, and one command installs everything on the Pi.

sections.heading: Backwards Heading Correction
sections.body: On the real robot, positive rotation from the mecanum mixer made the IMU heading decrease, so the heading correction pushed the wrong way. My simulation assumed they matched, which hid the mistake until the robot ran. I flipped the sign for the stock mixer, which leaves manual driving, motor inversion, and wiring as they were.

sections.heading: Overshooting the Turns
sections.body: With the sign fixed, the turns still overshot and hunted around each target, and more aggressive tuning made it worse. I added PID correction and capped power over the last 25 degrees of each turn, with the turn rate dropping toward the target and a slower recovery after any overshoot. A turn only finishes once the heading holds within 3 degrees, and on October 19, 2026 it completed all four turns in 3.4 to 3.7 seconds across five runs.

sections.heading: 502 Bad Gateway
sections.body: The dashboard could go down to a 502 Bad Gateway page. One cause was a power cut soon after OpenCV installed, which left its library incomplete and crashed every start, so the dashboard now tests OpenCV in a separate process first, repairs it when a camera is plugged in, and opens a recovery mode that shows the cause instead of a 502. The other was a fresh install aborting after it had stopped the dashboard, from an unset previous program variable. I fixed that variable, and a failed fresh install now starts the dashboard again.

sections.heading: Docs That Disagreed With the Wiring
sections.body: Some docs and code disagreed with the wiring diagram, like the servo board ground listed on pin 6 instead of pin 9 and the Mecanum sample's README swapping its left and right drivers. I corrected them and locked the reference wiring with tests that check every pin map and wiring table against it. The installer runs those tests, so a release whose wiring doesn't match the diagram won't install.

projects.title: PushBot
projects.summary: I wanted my old high school robot running again.
projects.cardSummary: PushBot is a small tank drive robot from my freshman or sophomore year of high school that I rewired so anyone can drive it from a phone browser with no app or internet. I rebuilt it around an ESP32-S3, two L298N drivers and a driver station the robot hosts itself. On battery alone the board restarts when Wi-Fi starts, and the motors don't turn even though every motor pin tests correctly. The code side is done, and what's left is a 5 V buck converter and fixing the power wiring to the drivers.
projects.imageAlt: PushBot, a 3D printed six wheel chassis with four yellow TT gear motors, two red L298N motor drivers and an ESP32-S3 on a screw terminal base.

overview.problem: The robot was broken and the old electronics were not worth fixing. I wanted to drive it from just a phone, with no app, computer, or internet, and have it safe enough to hand to someone else.
overview.method: I rewired it with a Lonely Binary ESP32-S3 on a screw terminal base and two L298N drivers, one for each side. The firmware runs the motors and also serves the driver station page, which has two thumb sticks I adapted from MotionModule.
overview.result: The driver station, Wi-Fi, and safety features all work, and the browser tests pass. It's still in progress because the motors are not turning yet and the board resets on battery power, and both come down to power wiring rather than code.

sections.heading: The Robot
sections.body: A 3D printed chassis carries six wheels, three per side, and four 5 V TT gear motors drive them through printed gears, two per side, so it steers like a tank. A 7 V battery powers the motors, and the right side is inverted in software because it's mounted as a mirror of the left.

sections.heading: Driver Station and Safety
sections.body: The left stick drives forward and back and the right stick turns, and a laptop can use WASD or a game controller. Driving needs a deliberate Enable, only one person can be in control, it starts at a 40% speed limit, and the motors ramp up instead of jerking. If commands stop for 500 ms, Wi-Fi drops, the page is left or the phone is rotated, the robot disables, and the board's RGB LED shows red for faults.

sections.heading: Phones and the Hotspot
sections.body: My first revival attempt was a PlatformIO version with an older pin map and power plan, which I replaced with the Arduino firmware in the repo now. Phones often dropped the robot's own Pushbot hotspot because it has no internet, so I added a Wi-Fi tab to save a home network, where PushBot shows up at pushbot.local. Away from home it falls back to its own network, and if the home network drops for 10 seconds the robot stops and the hotspot comes back.

sections.heading: Restarts on Battery Power
sections.body: With USB unplugged, the board restarts when Wi-Fi starts and the LED shows magenta for a brownout. The 5 V the L298N makes from the 7 V battery sags under the Wi-Fi current, and the board needs to stay above about 4.1 V during those bursts. Limiting transmit power to 8.5 dBm, slowing the CPU and restarting Wi-Fi at 2 dBm after a brownout only lower the load, so this isn't fixed yet. The real fix is a 5 V buck converter rated 2 A or more wired from the battery to the board's 5V and GND, or a USB power bank in its USB-C port, and the battery only test with a separate 5 V supply still has to confirm the cause.

sections.heading: Motors That Won't Turn
sections.body: In the last test the motors didn't turn at all. A pin test over USB showed every ESP32 motor pin switching the right way for forward and reverse, so the code side works and the problem is the driver power wiring, which isn't fixed yet. The next step is running the battery to each L298N's 12V screw with real wire clamped under the screws instead of jumper pins, and checking the driver LEDs stay lit with USB unplugged. The L298N also loses about 2 V, so the motors only see around 5 V at full power, and if the 40% starting limit is too low to get them moving the speed slider goes up. After that come the raised wheel direction test, two thumb driving on a real phone, and a first floor drive at 40% or less.

projects.title: Pi Camera Dashboard
projects.summary: I made this to fit MotionModule's dashboard style and updater into something much smaller.
projects.cardSummary: This is a small Raspberry Pi 4 dashboard I wrote that streams its camera and controls the case fan from any browser on the same Wi-Fi. It removes the need to SSH in to see the camera or change the fan. The main problem was the camera, since one plugged in or reseated after the dashboard started was never detected. The dashboard now checks for a camera from a fresh process and restarts itself once one appears, while fan control keeps working the whole time.
projects.imageAlt: The Camera & Cooling dashboard with the camera panel on the left and the CPU temperature with Auto, On and Off fan buttons on the right.

overview.problem: I wanted to see a Pi camera from my phone and keep the Pi cool without SSHing in every time something needed to change.
overview.method: I wrote it in plain Python with no Flask or extra web files, so the installer is the only setup. The camera streams at 720p, the fan switches on GPIO14, and the temperature check runs separately from the camera and browser so neither can take it down.
overview.result: It installs with one command, starts on boot, and does what I wanted. The camera, fan polarity, and install still need checking on real hardware, since the automated tests run without a Pi.

sections.heading: Cooling
sections.body: In Auto the fan turns on at 60°C and off at 50°C so it doesn't flicker around one temperature. Manual On and Off are available, but at 75°C the fan comes on anyway until the Pi drops back to 60°C, and it also turns on if the temperature can't be read.

sections.heading: Updates
sections.body: The dashboard checks GitHub for a newer commit every 15 minutes without downloading anything. Updating asks for the Pi's password, which goes to sudo and isn't saved. The update runs in its own systemd unit and rolls back to the previous release if the new one fails its health check.

sections.heading: Cameras Connected Late
sections.body: libcamera only looks for cameras once at startup, so a camera plugged in or reseated after the dashboard started was never found. Now with no camera the page explains how to reseat the ribbon, the fan keeps working, and the dashboard checks for a camera from a fresh process until one appears, then lets systemd restart it.

sections.heading: The Fan Pin and the Port
sections.body: GPIO14 is also the Pi's serial pin, and an existing fan setting could already be using it, so the install steps disable the serial console and other fan overlays and leave the dashboard as the only thing on GPIO14. The page also needed :8080 typed in, which is easy to forget on a phone, so it now serves on port 80 and only falls back to 8080 if 80 is taken.

projects.title: Promptagotchi
projects.summary: I wanted something always on screen, and fun to look at, that tells me which Claude Code session needs me.
projects.cardSummary: Promptagotchi is a pixel pet I built that sits on my screen and watches all of my Claude Code sessions. Instead of clicking through every window to find the one waiting on me, the pet waves a question mark when a session needs me and lets me answer permission prompts from it. The hard part was knowing what each session was actually doing, since Claude Code's status files can say busy while a session is waiting on a prompt. I added optional hooks that send live events to the pet, and a session with no news for 30 minutes is flagged as possibly waiting.
projects.imageAlt: Pip, an orange pixel pet, typing on its laptop next to the session list, where one session asks to run a command with Allow and Deny buttons.

overview.problem: I usually run several Claude Code sessions at once and was losing time checking each window for the one stuck on a prompt.
overview.method: I built it as a macOS app in Rust with Tauri, about 5 MB. It reads the status files Claude Code keeps for each session, and optional hooks send live details like the running tool, the current plan step, and subagents.
overview.result: It works on macOS with my own sessions. The pet floats over every app and full screen window without stealing focus, and clicking a session opens it in the Claude app, Terminal, iTerm2, or VS Code. It isn't notarized yet, and Windows, Linux, and Always allow from the pet are on the roadmap.

sections.heading: The Pet
sections.body: Pip is drawn on a 32 by 28 pixel grid with an animation for each state, typing while Claude works, waving under a question mark when a session needs me, hopping with a check mark when one finishes, and napping when idle. It docks to any edge or corner and scales to about 13% of the screen height. Two more pets come built in, and Pet Studio lets you draw your own frame by frame.

sections.heading: Watching the Sessions
sections.body: The app polls Claude Code's status folder once a second for each session's title, folder, and busy or idle state, with no setup. The optional hooks post events to a local server that requires a random token and rejects browser requests, and they run async so they never slow Claude down.

sections.heading: Answering From the Pet
sections.body: When a session asks for permission while I'm in another app, the pet shows Allow and Deny buttons, and multiple choice questions show their options. If I switch over or don't answer in 45 seconds, the prompt returns to Claude's window so nothing is lost. Prompts are shown but never saved, and everything stays on the computer.

sections.heading: Status Files That Said Busy
sections.body: The status files weren't reliable on their own. A desktop session waiting on a prompt could keep saying busy, so a session busy for 30 minutes with no news now stops the typing animation and is marked as possibly waiting, and a Stop from the hooks overrides a stale busy file. A turn that ended with a question also looked the same as a finished one, so the app reads the end of the session's transcript and shows ? instead of a check mark.

sections.heading: Hover Without Focus
sections.body: The pet's panels never take focus so they don't steal typing, but WebKit only tracks the mouse in the active window, so hovering did nothing. The Rust core now tracks the cursor itself and turns off click through only while it is over the pet or its cards.

projects.title: ProtoSpark Advanced CNC Course
projects.summary: I took ProtoSpark's Advanced CNC Course to learn to run an industrial CNC mill and lathe myself.
projects.cardSummary: I completed ProtoSpark's Advanced CNC Course in the Brooklyn Navy Yard, four weekly sessions on a Haas TM-1P mill and a Haas TL-2 lathe. It was a setup and machining course, not CAM, so the focus was setting up each job, running its operations and machining the part myself. The advanced course normally comes after the introductory one on Haas desktop machines, but the trainer looked at my CAD and design work and what I already knew about CNC and let me start in the advanced course. I finished able to set up and run both machines, with a milled bracket and a turned pawn to show for it.
projects.imageAlt: A machined aluminum bracket and a turned aluminum pawn from the ProtoSpark course, sitting on my desk.

overview.problem: ProtoSpark is a machine shop in the Brooklyn Navy Yard, and its Advanced Course is for people who want to use the industrial machines. Normally students take the introductory course first, but the trainer saw my CAD and design skills and my previous CNC experience and let me go straight into the advanced course.
overview.method: The course met once a week on September 19 and 26 and October 3 and 10, 2026, on a Haas TM-1P toolroom mill and a Haas TL-2 toolroom lathe. It was about setting up and running the machines rather than CAM. I learned how to set up a job, run its operations and mill the part, including G-code and loading work offsets.
overview.result: I finished the course able to run both machines. The bracket and the pawn in these photos are parts I machined there.

sections.heading: The Machines
sections.body: The mill was a Haas TM-1P, a three axis toolroom mill with 30 by 16 by 16 inches of travel, a 6,000 RPM spindle and a 10 pocket tool changer. The lathe was a Haas TL-2 toolroom lathe with a 1,800 RPM spindle and 48 inches of Z travel.

sections.heading: Setup, Operations and Machining
sections.body: Every job took more than one tool, so each part was split into operations with a different tool for each. Before a part was cut I set it up on the machine, loaded the tools and work offsets, then ran each operation in order until the part was finished.

sections.heading: The Milled Bracket
sections.body: The bracket came off the CNC mill. It has a large bore at one end, a smaller bore at the other, a long pocket with rounded ends between them, a step cut down one side, and broken edges all the way around.

sections.heading: The Turned Pawn
sections.body: The pawn came off the lathe. Its profile is a round head over a collar, a tapered stem that flares into the base, and a lip around the bottom, all cut on one axis.
